blocks.x: I'll make a note on here first that we are interviewing Mr. Edgar Joseph. Edgar Joseph. Your address is 1625 St. Philip. And the date is August the 7th, I guess. August 7th. Yeah, the 7th, 1961. That's right. And this is Bill Russell and Ralph Collins is also here at the interview. Do you mind giving me your full name again? Do you have any middle names?
No, they call me Joseph. My right name is Edgar Joseph.
Edgar Joseph.
That's right.
Do you have a nickname?
Sam, they call me for nickname. Sam, yeah. Yeah, this Sam like the nickname they call me.
I wonder if you mind telling just when you were born, what part of the city? I'm born in New Orleans. I'm born 1907.
What is the exact birth date? My name's birthday. Be what, I'm all? You? My name's birthday.
On 1907. Yeah.
What part of the city were you born in? Right here in New Orleans.
In New Orleans. New Orleans on St. Philip Street.
Right here? Right in the neighborhood. Right down there. Yeah.
New Orleans St. Philip. Yeah. That time it was the Rock, it was the Rock Street around here. A lot of musicians, there came well, there's still a lot of musicians around here.
Yeah.
Yeah, that's right. And all.

Eddie Morris, you say, lives right across the street. Right across the street on that side there. I remember when Kid Howard lived there. Howard used to live in H Block down there. Yeah, sir. And Jim and George Lurit. Jim used to live down there, all of them. Yeah, right there. Can you tell us about anyone in your family that ever played music that your father... Yeah, no.
My cousin Pratt, he played with Chris Kelly. He's dead. He played with Chris Kelly. He used to play with Papa Celestan too. And he played with Kid René.
What's he playing again?
Banjo. Banjo.
I got his picture, you want to see it? Yeah.
Right on the get it.
That's a picture.
What did you get? You're still a little fella, young man. That's him right there.
Oh, yeah.
Oh, yeah.
Wilfred Pratt, they called him.
Wilfred?
Wilfred Pratt. Right. That's him. Yeah. He's a little banjo player, man.
What was that take, right around here?
Right on Roman Street, right between the main and the synapse.
Yeah, he looks kind of familiar.
Yeah, and it's a nice picture. Yeah. I wonder if we could maybe snap a picture of that. Yeah, he looks like quite a young man there.
When was this taken about? Oh, that's taken a good while ago.
He was a popular man, man. Wilfred Pratt. I liked to get him too. He had a chance to get that full independent music.
You can keep talking around and get the tape running. Yeah.

You say he played with Chris Kelly, won't you? Played with Chris Kelly. He played with Papa Celestan. He played with Kid René. He used to play with old man Robichoux. Oh, yeah? Yeah, he played with old man Robichoux.
Just, they played the banjo, you see? Did he play guitar? Yeah. Yeah. Did he play guitar? And banjo, just banjo.
Just banjo. He used to play with Gaillet. Gaillet's the one shooting. Oh, yeah. Remember Gaillet got killed? Yeah. Gaillet's the one shooting. Oh.
And when was Eddie Craig with Kelly? About in the 20s?
Oh, it was about the 20s. Right after Kelly died, lay him out on the sand between Trayvon and Robinson in the middle on that side of the bank. He had a big few of himself stand. He did?
That's right.
He must have been very popular.
He was.
One of the best. He was a short trumpet like that. He had a short trumpet?
Yeah, he had a short one. I had one too.
I got rid of it. You know the little small horn like that? I got rid of it.
Did he play it too? No, he didn't play it when he had it.
He was all right. He was a good banjo player. Daddy respect him. He come to John the days when John Morales, you remember John Morales.
Oh, yeah, yeah.
Well, that's the time he come up. Oh, oh. You know.
Did you play with him?
I used to go with him. I was just starting out on the horn with him.
Oh, yeah.

And I played around here with Rene, Kid Rene. On the parade. A lot of young men too. Played with Rene. We run parades. I played with Lee Collins, who he's dead too. Oh, yeah. I worked with Lee Collins at the La Vida and all. Oh, yeah. Because Alan Conner, that time he was upstairs with George McCubbin and all that bunch. Alvin Alcon. Oh, yeah. Alvin's brother I used to work with.
Oh, Alvin's brother? What's his name?
George McCubbin they called him. He's dead.
Oh, that's Alvin's brother? Yeah, that's half brother. Half brother, yeah.
Half brother. Now, Alvin's right brother.
Well, George McCullin, he was the son of the old George McCullin, wasn't he? Yeah, that's right.
The dad was a trumpet player too. Yeah. That's the old man, he used to live on Louisiana Avenue, which when he lived there.
I'm up there, you know.
Well, yeah, there's a lot of confusion there, but there's a junior and a senior. Well, he got a son now.
A son and a daughter playing. I know his son is playing. I know his son, Lola, his wife they call her Lola.
Nola. That's George McCullin Jr. Yeah, that's right.
She had a whole lot of good records too, George. He was a good man. That man couldn't, the only way he played his horn he had to be drunk. He lost about nine horns on street cars.
Oh, dear. That's right. Let's talk a little more about you and Gil while we're here.
Well, to finish telling you, I got around here with all them old time musicians. I played with, uh...
Were you telling us about any other relations that ever played music?
Well, none of my other relations.
Not your mother or...
No, my mother didn't know, uh-uh. Not my father. None of my father needed my mother, needed my daddy.
Well, how come you started to take off the music?
Well, I took it up with old man Shao Ney on St. Gloria.
Oh, yeah?
Had two bits of lessons.
Well...

Well, he come from, you know, he come from school. Sometime I wasn't there two bits of go play. I lied to him I went to music lessons. Same time I didn't go. He's right down St. Gloria Street, old man Shao Ney. He learned white and colored too. White and colored. He was a good old teacher. See, before I pick up a horn, yeah, I take you, he used to get you like that, make your concert time. One, two, three, make you sing your notes. Uh-huh. First piece of music I learned how to play, when the saints go much in the middle of my God today, with him. Oh, yeah. That's why you could play. And you didn't play your horn right away. You didn't get a horn, just make a horn up and play it right away like some people do. Uh-huh. You didn't do that with him. Uh-huh. You had to wait till you make your chords, hum the notes. A, B, C, D, D, G, A, all of that. Oh, yeah. You had hum the notes to him, you understand? You couldn't just say you want to play. One night we was all in there, he's sitting back in the kitchen. We tried to make up, you know, try to play some music in there. Uh-uh. They used to call him a pet. Did you get it, Bill? Yes, I think so. Okay, thank you.
What did they call him again?

They used to call him a pet. My pet, Shauna. Oh, my pet. Yeah, my pet used to call him. What do you get, a little pitch of wine? He'd sit on the side of us and go in there, all right, boys. Get there, get your horn together, take your man, take your knee. Why the jerk, you know, make the straight leg like that, you know? Oh, yeah. You tell people like this, it sounds funny. Oh, all right. And so, you sit down there by him. You come there wrong, you know what he tell you? Go back home.
And you didn't get to blow your horn at all? No, you didn't blow no horn right away.
You didn't blow no horn about four or five weeks before you went there. Well, did you take your horn?
Yeah, you took a horn.
But he wouldn't let you play your horn, you understand? He make your hummler notes. Like he makes a sing note. A, B, C, D, E, R, all that. He make you sing all that. Yeah, sing it hummler with him.
But you didn't take your case? Yeah, I had my case right there,

which you could not take that one out to play nothing. You couldn't take it out? No. He'd take the time and he'd make you sit down there and he'd ask you questions. And now he'd ask you how many notes in music and how you divide the music. What are seven notes in music? In other words, four notes. You understand? You can make more than that. He'd ask you all them questions like that. Well, sometimes you'd have your mind, he kept you on a snap journey, he'd catch you sometimes. You understand what I mean? Yeah. Well, he know why he'd catch you. He know you ain't been doing it studying your horn. Yeah. And after you get there, you get there, you go home, man, get home, try to play, blow, blow. First thing, he'd own a little old scale out for the mirror of my guard to be. First piece of music to play with him. We're at home, blow, blow, blow, blow, blow. Man, you learn that? Man, it's always the hardest thing in the world after you learn that through a piece of it. So, come back to you and say, well, I'm going to try it. See, can you play this? You think you're going to play something? You make all the boys get their horn. About six of us. Get your horn. Guess what you put on on you? When the same girl marching in. Don, don, don, don, don. The clarinets, trumpets. He'd have all that cleat teeth. Clarinet, trumpets, bass drum, violin. All students. All students, right there in the house. All bunch of youngsters.
Can you remember who else was studying with you at that time?

Gilbert Young was going there too. You know Gilbert Young? Yeah. Wake up at the post office. Gilbert used to be the worst one in the bunch. Oh, man, I had trouble with Gilbert. See, his son Gilbert would take lessons. You know what he'd do, Bill? Gilbert would spend his money. That time Gilbert was living on, yeah. Gilbert used to be, you know like all kids. Gilbert would go to the show. I ain't lie, I would go to the show too. I went to the show too. Take the horn, go in the show. Come back, go, yeah, I went to the lesson. At the same time I'd be lying, I was lying. I ain't even say I didn't lie. I ain't lied to him. We used to do that. So, we got into him. Said, let's make up my mind. This man, we might have to go ahead. What he was the only one you could pay two bits of lessons. See, that other fellow was showing you a dollar and something. You know, that time they had a fellow in the town they called a fair boys. He was charging a dollar and something was going to get lessons. And they had a Monetta, across the, you know, Fest. Well, Fest was charging kind of high, especially with a lot of them white boys across the river. Well, we couldn't fool Fest, that really was too much. And I'll tell you another story I took and done. I learned how to get my horn really good. I got around them old mans. So, I say to myself, I'm going to do something with this horn right now. I get all them old time musicians. I even got with Schatz. You know Schatz was a good trumpet player. Yeah, I heard it. Right behind Lewis. So, one Sunday Schatz called me up and said, I got to pray. I'll never forget a jolly boy pray. Say, hey you can make it? I said, yeah, I can make it. Man, I didn't know if I could make it. I went just the same.
I went with Schatz, man.
I done one of them. So, after, come in and I get there. Man, I had, boy, you making a whole lot of noise. That time I had that little short, doing a little short trumpet like that.
Burn that, son.

Yeah. When I was doing trenchment work, I find horn and I passed the horn up myself. I passed the horn up. Sheep would tell you the same thing. Sheep had an old horn too. I'll tell you about this. Same time, when everybody's on the story, that, Sheep had an old horn, it was patched. It was all bent up. When I took the horn apart, I was doing metal work. I could do it good. I fixed the horn up. Yeah, not the horn could pick Howard. What Howard took and done. Howard took and, after I fixed the horn for Sheep, Howard took the horn. Sheep come out of these horns from Howard, Howard had a job to go play at night. She tell you about that. So, him and Howard had it. So, I said, Sheep, Howard, I learned you my horn. I learned Sheep, Howard my horn. But Howard was good too, you understand? Well Howard had done good towards me too. Howard hired me too. So, only one, I asked him, think back. I turned around there. I goes on a, this is my cousin. I goes with, with Lambry. You remember Lambry, you played with old Rickum? He gets the old, the Eleanor's. You know the Eleanor's uptown, I don't know what to say. So, I call him, for the days they like to call him. Lambry said, you want to make, you want to make a couple of hours. Yeah, I'm making. Man, I started with Lambry around about 11.30. Man, my lift got so weak, and I started to come on home. I told Lambry, I can't make it no more. I said, don't be scared boy, don't be scared. So, man, I took him, you know, drink maybe by drinking, and maybe, maybe, you made me come up and bat him. So, I said, 12 o'clock, we was up around, uh, Louisiana. You know where they make the town come down, St. Charles. I said, Chef, they didn't even use me going to myself. I said, they didn't use me going back home. I got to St. Charles, and St. Charles and Louisiana. I said to myself, I said, I'm going to put it in the good Lord's hand. I'm going to try to make it. And man, do you know I made it? I made it. I come all the way down to Canal Street. That time we had to go to Canal Street and come back up and walk it. Long way. Long way. Well, we made a stop on Magazine. Somewhere around St. George Street, there's a feeders up there, you know. They give us something neat. So, Lamb said, you know how you feel better now, boy? I said, yeah, man, I felt good. When they hit Napoleon Avenue, going out towards South Street, you understand? I felt more better, you understand what I mean? When they hit it way up around Nashville. Man, I can make another one like that again tomorrow. Make another one like that. That's how I begin to make myself. You understand what I'm doing? So, after another boy, I started playing with George E. Parker at the Happy Landing. I tell you, see me, I had plenty of knowledge. So, at night the union had, was 12 fans at the Jitsa Tea Room. Jitsa Tea Room. With George E. Parker, I played with George E. Parker. I had me, George E. Parker, Michael Lee. This boy played guitar. I know you didn't even heard about him. He drive the lumber truck back in town. Ruben, Ruben they called him. Ruben, Ruben can tell you. Well, we had about nine pieces. And Dave, well, Dave Van was up there too playing. And so, Dave, uh, Dave was telling me. So, I'm going to tell you, man, I got up there. Mike, I swear to Jesus Christ, boys and boys there. And Bigfoot Billy was with it. Stay down to another man, you should be asking me that. So, Mike, Mike seen Dave with Dave Van. Dave played a couple of them. I said, no lie, Mike, I'm not lying. Mike in California. Mike packed up his home and said, man, I ain't playing against that band. I said, what's the matter? I said, you getting paid like it, boys. Man, I know where I got the strength at. In the same building, I got up and I got against Dave. Me and Dave had it. So, people come up there. So, Mike, little music, come up there. I said, I didn't know you could do that. I said, many things I can do, I can't do, I tried myself in doing it, playing music. You understand what I mean? So, that got all right. Well, after we finished, the youths had come up. All the band had to play about three hours to play. And the way the union was funded to music, to build money for the union. You understand what I mean? But the union wasn't like it is now. The union didn't have the money like they got now. You understand what I mean? So, turned around there. We turned around. I get the job at the Masonic Temple on St. Charles. On the 14th floor up there. I played up there for some American Can Company, some big shot of the American Can Company. They got a beautiful stand up. You know, if you haven't been up there and seen them stand up there. We played up there. Who they had up there? They had Rush for the pair of units and Tony Albarico. Oh, yeah. Three bands up there. Now, you know, I had some of them boys with us. I had some boys with them bands.
Man, you could let them go in the store there.
Man, you worried about them, man.
They come up here to make money.

We ain't talking about them, man. We looking to make money like they're making. So, we made it on that. Turn around from that. They hired me. I played at the World Convention. I wish I had that picture to show you. I had a book of me. The whole village, I'll tell you who was playing with me. Boy was like John Cleo. You remember Cleo? He played bass? Oh, yeah. He played with Howard. He had Cleo. You remember Tato? Oh, yeah. Point of that. Point of that. Point of that. Point of that. Altar. Altar, yeah. Had his blood on the piano. And had a boy that called Paul Antwine. And Harmon Antwine. We played at the World Convention. Tony Albarico was downstairs and we was upstairs. Well, we played. Man. Man.
If you want to stop at any time, go ahead. No, wait, I was at Valor.

In the finish time we leave there. We leave off the new ferry boat. We go to New Orleans Airport. And play it again. We played that night that day. So them boys, you know what people do? I just wish I had the book to show you. Man, they bought us everything. They took all kinds of pictures of us. Cleo was riding the bass. You know Cleo was taking a ride to the bass and play it like that. And well, made it on that. I made it on that turnaround. I get to another job. Same company I work for. The Acme Insurance Company. I played at the Junk Hotel for them. Well, everywhere I went, they had white bands. And that's what gave me courage to bring me up on, not to be scared to play my horn with nobody.
Sure, that's good. See?

You got fellas that's playing. You know they see another band, they get scared. Well, I'm not scared of nobody. If a man's better than me, he's this better than me. That's what I was thinking. Sure. You understand what I mean? I'll take it like that. If you better than me, I ain't gonna say nothing. Well, someday I might catch up with you. You understand what I mean? I might catch up with you. I don't say I'm no star. You understand what I mean? Well, I'm gonna do my part when I'm supposed to do. And right now the band I got, I got a band. I got a good set up of boys. I ain't got no youngsters, I'll tell you what I got. I use Bigfoot Billy. I use Charlie Anthony. Charlie Hamilton?
Yeah, piano player.

Played piano with me. I used Homer Lejean. He played his great guitar and trombone. When Clement not playing at the Paradise, I used him on bass with me. That's the kind of band I got. And don't you think them old man can play? Them old man really play some music. You understand what I mean? Sure. What I like about them, them, them youngsters is alright. But they don't even beat them old man. See now, like we got a dance at the Auto Crack Out Club, the Lions Club. Well, we got the down in our seat, they got a big 14 band. 14 piece band, you know. All you can sign. See, it's 14 pieces of music. I take six pieces and run them in the river with it. That's right.
What do you think makes the difference between the young man and the old man?

What do you think the old man know what they're doing better than the youngsters? The youngsters, you see the youngsters, they take and they want to do, they want to do too much. They want to do too many things. It's only one thing you can do when you're playing music. Sit down and try to play a straight lead and play your horn right. With all that monkey shine, you don't be doing that. See them jumping off the bandstand with a horn in your mouth, enough for you to fall off a stadium and cripple yourself with that. You know it yourself. I know a bunch of them white boys the same. Them white boys, all them boys on the street don't do that. They play the horn like they're like the color sound they play like they're supposed to play. You understand what I mean? Sound played like that. When you're going to get to jumping and all that and throwing, jumping off a chair, you
don't be doing that.

Right. Not playing music, putting on a show. That's right. That's what they call putting on a show. But that's still not playing your horn like they're supposed to be playing. See? Now, I look at some of them fellas. I got fellas with me and I see them fellas, they can play and they know what they're doing. They never catch them crying. They don't play that part where they're supposed to play. See? Now you see at Andrew Higgins' house, I used to play up there too up on Patanian Street. You know Patanian, before you get to the Jackson? Yeah. It was a corner, we played for them. I played a whole lot of crowd doing the big, big dances for them. And the holidays, you understand me Bill? No. Well they had treated us, wonderful. Of course, and I played for them people and I played for them people. I didn't make no price with them. I supposed to get off at 2, you know what time I got off? 6 o'clock in the morning. They said, just go ahead and play whatever it is, I'll make up the difference. Now they got a white fella, Mr. Wagman, right behind the country club. You know, nobody knew on the country club. Country club's on that side, you got a house on that side. Well every year I played his daughter, Devil Jude, dance. I bet the house. Well we don't start till around quarter to 10. Well that dance lasts till 6, 7 o'clock in each morning. That's the kind of jobs I get with them kind of people. And the people that are playing for them people, they never ask you nothing. You understand what I mean Bill? All they want you is give them respect and kind and give them the music that they want to. When they start drinking and they want to dance, you got to just feel like they want to dance. You understand, you can't just stop, get tired and say, well, we're taking an intermission. When we start late like that, we don't take no intermission. We're ready for them to tell us to relax a while, let them rest, and we go to playing again. That's how we get along with the people. I get all my gear with the people. And anywhere I went, I would try to satisfy anybody. Now, about a week ago we played up here on the Poison Avenue. I know if you've ever been in there, the Jewish club. Up on the Poison Avenue? It's between Magazine and 8th Street and the Miller Block. They got a beautiful hall. You been in there?
No, I don't think so.

It's a beautiful place. All air conditioning in there. They got around about 500 small tables. I know the Acme Insurance Company is fixing to give their Christmas card up there. I told them about a place. They asked me where they think they'd be able to get a place. And when I was charging my band, I told them what I asked them. Well, for them, I charged them $135 for seven pieces of music. That's a Christmas party. Now, every year I played by Miss Commander. You ever been there?
No.
You ever been there? No, I never been there either.
Like in Washington Avenue? Yeah, I know the place. It's a big gift.

I can tell you what. I played all the dance every Christmas for them. She got something, man, I swear you all will see. You ever see heat in it? You know how cold it is last year? How cold it is? Yeah. She got in the yard, they got lights, heat in the yard. It's like summertime.
Yeah.

That's why these men, you see they come over like this. Cover it over, huh? No, they don't cover it over. It's like this. About this wide. See about three inches wide. You understand what I mean? They got gas lights in them. Oh, yeah. Oh, man, that thing be so warm. The same Billy can tell you. All that boy Charlie Hammond tell you, they had Darcy with me on the beach up there. Oh, yeah. And, man, they were so hot in that yard, and they was freezing outside. They were really freezing out there.
That's the first time I've ever seen anything like that. First time I've ever seen anything like that.

Well, me, last time the princess said, we couldn't play out in the yard, but this year, they said we can give you all that yard. We didn't play upstairs. They got a beautiful dance hall upstairs. They called him this morning. And Mr. Commander, he can tell you about me, Mr. Adam, Mr. Joseph. Every year I get that job. Sign a contract. Every year. Nobody else. But I use seven pieces with him. He's very nice. And, man, he got something there. I never seen nothing like that in my life. You see how that guy's been heat like heat work in the yard when it's open.
Yeah, that's really something.
I wish you, Niesty, the Garth family, Niesty, when I play up there, I'm going to try to get in touch with y'all and let y'all come up there and make a picture. Yeah.
I'd like to see that.

I'd like you to see that, see how that thing, how that heat gets there. You can come in there. I've seen some pictures of the inside. Inside. What he wins the prize every year on the best Christmas lights. You think he must cost him money? He gets them big, you know them big cranes that put them lights, neon lights all night. He put them cranes to put them lights in. It's beautiful to see. What he had farms and all that. You understand me? Well, nothing to catch you on the fire. Next time I'm in there, they said, God spared me from living. I'm going to get in touch with y'all and have y'all come up there. Christmas fall on Sunday, whatever it's falling on, I'll let you know and y'all come up there. Y'all going to be my guests until I know I'm going to have some guests come up there. All right. I even had the priestess dancing up there. Cali priests, well they come to me. They ask me a question, because I'm Cali too, you see, and I belong to 90 feet of Cleveland. We got a place on Arlene Street. We just come to this shit man. He said, Joseph? I don't dance, but I'm dancing this music. You know where he danced, what he made us do. He got there and made a parade out of it. We played the same group marching, and I had Eddie Johnson with me, work by Worldline, you know Eddie Johnson. Ask Eddie. He made us march all to the bottom, and guess who was the grand march? The priest. The priest and some ladies with man, and man, you're a fella I haven't seen that man, the priest, and nobody on like that look. Going around there. I said, look at her, and she's jessing there. I said, what? Man, I wish y'all would have been there where you could snap a picture of that. Man, you would love to see something like that. Do you understand me? That's the first time I haven't seen anything like that.
Well, I guess that Jeezy just made him feel good. That's right.

You'd be surprised when you knew some people. You know what he told me? He told me, he told me, he said, well I just come in Joseph. He's from New York. He said, I've been around places, but I've never seen a place. Mr. Commander got us to play, and the same girl watching him for about nine times. So then, Mr. Moran told him, he's gonna show him, how he makes the carnival parades down there. Well, all the guests, white girls and white boys, they're all in applause. They got the girlfriend, man, and we playing watching with him. Man, that was something good to see. So now I didn't see something like that. That was really good. They have nice parties. Now, other thing, I had played on these little appetizers, nice to play every Sunday for the Hawks at the center centers. Well, they have a dance, nice to play the appetizers too. When was that? How long ago was that? Oh, that's a good while ago. That's about three months ago. Oh, three months?
Three months ago.
That time, we used to have bands and trucks. You understand what I mean?
Well, I remember too.
About six pieces, riding around the truck. You see, they go around, riding cars.
You did that just three months ago? Yeah, yeah. Oh, I didn't know.
Do that, going around different places like that, and appetizing, you understand, for the dance.
You were on the truck?

Yeah, I still... On your band? No, we used six pieces like that. Six pieces. We'd ride around the truck, go maybe uptown. We leave from uptown, come down, Burgundy. And when we coming in, going to the center center, where we start the plane from Yale, playing either the same group marching in, with the truck going slow. And they make like a parade. Oh, you're riding in the house, huh? Yeah, they make a parade out of it. You'd be surprised how much kick that is. Water truck be going slow at the same time, you understand what I mean? And man,
Billy do me so good sometimes, when I see them boys having fun like that.

Sometimes I'm sorry when it's over. Yeah. You know, I'll be enjoying myself. Sure. I'll be enjoying myself just like it's me down there. Smeet Army. Bo said, we in Moikin. And all them boys in the band, they like that too. See, that's what makes a band.
Makes people happy.

That makes people happy and that makes your band. It's the best thing in the world to be with a bunch of man, everybody agreed at one point. But if you got Contreras fellas in the band, you never have a band. See?
Imagine fellas.

See, you got fellas, you got some fellas sometimes, they get stared, they argue about the money. You understand what I mean? I never make no argue about no money. When I go do my business, I do my business in the business way. I'm going to sign a contract and I'll pay them off. You understand what I mean? And I don't want nobody to tell me how they're doing, what they're doing, what not to do. Now if you hire me to do something, I'm going to do like you tell me in your band.
See?

I'm not going to, you see, nothing of a thing. You see plenty of people understand this. When you're playing music, you see these people, when they're people hire you, you know these people don't have to give you nothing to eat and nothing to drink.
You understand what I'm talking about?

They ain't got to give you a glass of water. You understand? Them people is paying you to play. Now if they want to give you water, they give you water. You understand what I mean? They feel like giving you water, they give you water. Before I make the people give you nothing, them people ain't supposed to give you nothing. They ain't supposed to give you nothing. What you got some fellas playing, they're talking, man, why don't you ask a man to give me a bottle, can't get us a drink. You know what I tell them? I tell them all I'm brought in the back. I say, look, y'all going on the job. If you want to stop and get you something to drink, y'all better buy you something to drink. Now don't ask me to ask the people for nothing to drink, and they don't ask me for nothing to drink. Now if they give us, we'll take it. But if you don't give us, I can't get mad with you. You know why? I'm charging, you paying me, and I can buy what I want after. When I knock off, I buy what I want. You understand what I mean, Bill? Well, I can't just go make you give me things like that. When you got plenty of fellas, they be inspecting all that.

They be expecting you to make the people give you something, which you cannot. Now sometimes, you play for the people and they're hungry. You need to ask people to make the sandwich. Well, I feel embarrassed to be asking people about something easy. See, I always get up. It's supposed to tell me, no, I can't get mad. You know what, I'm charging enough to get you on your own lunch. Now if you give me something, I'll appreciate it. If you don't give me nothing, it's alright, it's the same with me. When I knock off, I'll go out and maybe buy me something. What I say, I work with Paul Barberand. I've been all around the country with Paul Barberand. He's the same way, been with him. And I like Paul for this. I'll catch Paul, anywhere Paul, play. You never catch Paul. Ask nobody for nothing to drink. They give Paul, it's alright. As far as him asking the people to give, no. I played at New Orleans Country Club with Paul. We didn't ask for nothing. The man said, Paul, y'all take intermission, come on. We'll give y'all, speak something for the band. As far as asking, we didn't ask for nothing. And that's what Paul liked about me. Paul tell you the same thing. As long as I was really good with playing with him. We never ask nobody for nothing. We never get out of our place with nobody playing music. We try to satisfy the people. You understand me, Bill? Every person come and ask me, do you know this? If one of us don't know it, it's somebody in that band knows it. You see, like Eddie Johnson, Eddie Johnson knows every number, every number you ask for, Eddie can give it to you. With Eddie, it's got all kinds of music in there. He's a good saxophone player. He's a good man. He's a good man. And what I like about Eddie, he's old. Eddie's got some good remember-bill. Eddie can bring some things up to you sometimes with music, you'll be surprised. That's right. He makes you play your horn. It's the number they bring up to you, and after everybody's falling in, it makes you play your horn. It gives you a feeling when you've got a man in there. What you going to do with a bunch of youngsters in the band? You've got a bunch of, all they know is bebop. All they bebop.
You see, a bebop, you know, they know it'll get you nowhere.
But you know, you see that's getting out of style? Yeah, I think so. That's getting out of style.
See, people know, you can't, all right, now you're going houses.

Right now, some of them people call me up here, they say, George, I'd like to get your band. Why don't I get four pieces? Well, I'll say you've got four pieces, and then I'll tell them whatever it costs. You understand me? You know what they tell me? We don't, we ain't got no big house. We want a house for the musicians in the house, in about four or five-room house. You understand me? What you see, you can take three pieces of music, four pieces of music, and make this much out of the four, you make out of ten pieces. If you've got the right kind of man's weight, what you understand what I mean? And that's what the people want. And that's most of all my job like that.
Most of all my job work like that. That's like private parties.

That's right, that's right. Now, we got, you know, I got me coming, about two Saturdays from now, I'm going over to Lake at the concert club over there. Oh, yeah. They had St. Louis concert club, I used to go over there before. Well, I'm in Manhattan, what he's paying is a good price and all. Well, like I told him, man, he had asked me, could I have more pieces? I told him, he's all right with me. He wanted, I used to go over there with six, he wanted to bring eight. So the last time I went over there, he said, Jules, you better bring your six piece back. I'm going to tell you what the man told me. Now, listen at me, because you all people know it. He said, you got two man up there, the man's not playing. Now, he said, I'll show you how the man knows what you're doing. I said, what you mean? He said, the saxophone over there, that man's not playing. The other saxophone player, he's not playing. He just make one go, and he takes his own. This man is playing. What he's talking about there, do you understand what I mean? Well, he said, you better bring the little band like this. Now, he hired me, told him to bring the little small band. The man made, I knew what they were doing, but the man made me feel so embarrassed. You understand what I mean? I couldn't open my mind. All I had to say was yes. You understand what I mean? I knew that. And you see a big band, and you take it, you know you all been around. You see a big band with ten or twelve pieces? All them, all them going to be playing in that band? They're about six or seven playing in that band. You understand what I mean? It's four man's, it's not doing nothing in that band. What they're expecting the same money, what the other fellas is getting. You understand? Well, and people ain't nobody at school anymore. No. People ain't nobody at school. See a piano player? He's all the time working. A drum player, a good drum player, he's got the way. A guitar player, he's got the way. A man playing trumpet, he's got the way. What's he three sides for him? They ain't got the way going. No, they ain't got the way going. A man playing bass, he's got the way. See, he's got to be whore. And he know he's working. We see him three sides for him. They ain't three three trumpets. It's one of them trumpets that ain't doing nothing in that.
That's right.

You set aside and you see. You can tell a different. And then that's so, I'm the wisest in town like I've been running to my little band. I'm on to many of them fellas. Many fellas say I try to be hard, but I'm not no hard fella. See, when a man hire me, I'm going to try and give a man service. I want to come back to a man. I don't want to never go back to the same man. I make me feel proud to go back. Well, if I go there doing it wrong, I'm never going to go back to the man. He's my wrong. See, the man's going to say, you done me a little dirty trick. He'll tell me one of these, he'll say, you know why I'll get you no more? You done me a little dirty trick. Alright. Tell you what that happened. Now, I played Espinade and Dauphine for Ms. Claiborne Williams. You heard of her? Oh, yeah. She's in the City Hall. Well, she's good friends with the people I work for. Mr. Robach, she's living over in St. Louis right now. They call her Claiborne Williams. Stay right there from me in Dauphine, the house upstairs, the big house. They got a whole lot of old colored folks stay with them, dance with Red Rays. We played the big dance and that for them. Man, them people treat us so fine. And I had, what the only thing made me bad with me, made me out. I have to tell you, I had them done me a little dirty trick. I had Emma, Emma, Emma the sweet, the bell go with you and her. You know what she done me, Bill? It's nothing good.
I'm playing.

Well, I went, you know, over there in the back, went in the laboratory. She didn't know I know the people. Man, she came out about her card. So she said, Ms. Claiborne Williams said, Joseph, this ain't your card. This is Emma, Emma the bell girl. I looked at her and said, Emma. I said, I really don't like what you took and done. Well, I told her. I didn't want to make no disturb. I wasn't telling people in the house. I said, Emma, I don't think I like what you done. I said, I think you're wrong. So, I said, Emma, I'll tell you what you can do. I stayed after. We didn't have to go to about one thing. I'd have to stay there. Well, she made $27 with me. So, she lived way up and around, open around, up and around Cherokee and up in Colton. Well, I had Sam call that got there for the company. I got the canal ramp. I said, Emma, that's the four. She said, I thought you were gonna take me home. I said, no. I said, that's the four you get your call. Get your two-lane call to go home. I said, you know why I done you that? I didn't wanna make dogs and make myself shame in front of people. Then people know me better than know her, you understand? I make a muck out of myself. I said, you're tooken past cards on my job. Oh, not me, not me. I said, here's your card, yeah. And she told, she told Pussy, all them fellas, I'd say in all them. She said, you're the average, he done me a rotten trick. I said, she didn't tell you what she done, was trying to pass cards on my job. You understand me? Pass cards on my job. I didn't say nothing. I said, hello, hello. With Foy getting away from me, she came away. If I couldn't get Charlie Hampton, you know, I take them to hire another brilliant instrument in it. I put a sack on for that for hire. You understand, you're putting a piece of bread in the Pussy and Moth.
Yeah, that sounds right. You passing cards on, man. Do you think it's right? No. I don't think it's right. You understand what I mean? Now, I never know me that too.

That's my little cousin, man. Course is way over in South America, Andy. You know Andy, say, here I play. John Handley. John Handley. John Handley was over late with me too. I had a good job over there. I was on Saturday. Man, when I go to the laboratory, man, man showed me a call.
I said, now you're not his, fellas.
You're trying to pray anyway, and they're trying to hurt me. I didn't know.
That night he finished playing. Give him his money.
He didn't tell him nothing. So he called me again and said, you're not my money.
I'm going over there to say.
I said, oh no, man, you're not going over with me. And no Oscar Lewis. You know Oscar Lewis, man. Delegate of the one with the glass. Little Oscar Lewis, you know. Ask Oscar. I called up Oscar.
I asked Oscar, be ready for Saturday night.

We're going over the lake. I take Oscar over there. See? You know that Oscar's glad to make that money. I said, man, next time you got to don't forget me. Call on me. You understand me? Well, he's a man. He realized a man. A man is giving you a piece of bread and you try and do him. Do you call yourself a friend? No. Eh? As much of them fellas really been around here. Yet they don't get no jobs. And thanks I get jobs from some big people. I get jobs. Most of my jobs are all white. You know what I mean? Most of my jobs are strictly white. job is stricter white. And I get good jobs, I get no funny jobs. See, I don't fool them. I don't fool them. You know, I know what's the result of the colored people, you understand
what I mean? Do the colored people like this old style of music? Do you think they really like it

now? No, they're not so much. I know. They run little rock and roll stuff. You understand what I mean? Younger runs, anyway. Yeah, the youngest one. And now the young colored people, you know what they tell you, when you can't play that, you can't play nothing. And that rock and roll, you know what that is? See, rock and roll, that's not, that music been out before I was born, before you were born. And it's like a long time like Charleston. You remember Charleston? You remember all that old thing like that? That's what they used to play all that before. They call it, now they call it the rock and roll. The, what you call this, the zip, the zip, and the jump and all
that stuff. You understand? All that music been out before, they were 12 years old.

Sure. Now you see like, like them times like, they're saying about my cousin, they used to play all that kind of music. That time people used to go for that blue. They used to go, the color used to go for all that. But now they don't go for that. They don't want all that little rock and roll stuff. And I don't see no sense in it. All they're just doing is killing yourself. They're killing themselves. They're jumping around you, they're soaking wet. Yeah, that's right. They'd be soaking wet. You understand? You go around and say, why
the people you can't play, they can't hear them for me. They say, oh, we want you to

play regular style music. Dance music where they can dance. Yeah, that's right. Dance music. They want dance music. You understand me? What did you want people to tell you that? They don't want to have to tell you that twice. You understand? They come back and they'll stop you. Told you if you can't play that, don't play at all. You're feeling bad. You can't play what you want, you got to play what the people want. And when you satisfy the people in audience, when you're playing music, that's the best thing in the world. Now, you don't go there to play music for yourself like you want, no. You don't be doing that. You got to play to satisfy them people. What do they like best? Waltzes, Fox stars? They like waltzes. Planet White like waltzes. They like that. The color like that too. They like waltzes too. Well, I'll tell you the truth. You see waltzes? That's sweet music, man. That's sweet music, waltzes. Let me call you sweetheart. One rose, two old dreams and all that stuff. That's all nice music. I'll tell you the thing, to my narrative, I'd rather play all that all night long. All of that one rose and a four-leaf clover. That's nice music. You can play that in the waltz time, you can play in the foxstrap time. You understand what I mean Bill? And people enjoy it.
But you play it as a waltz first and then? You play it off in the waltz. And you turn it

around and you jump it. And you jump it in the foxstrap time. And you dance a little faster. You understand how you go to two steps. Well, the people get used to make waltzes in the two steps too. People enjoy that. What you going to get to that? Don't play them kind of things for some new college, man. You going to play waltzes for them. We played at Pickley for the 20th last Sunday. We went to Good Citizen Ranch over there. Man, that's all the people want. We play waltzes. We played most waltzes all day. What I tell you I had on there. I had Eddie Johnson. I had Manuel Serra's on Ghetto. They didn't use these bands. They used Ghetto on Converse Show. Bigfoot, Billy, myself. We played all that, man. And people enjoyed that. Waltzes and when the saints go marching in the close to the walk of Jesus. Well, they got around, you know, marching all out in the field. And the rain come down and made them out of getting to eat that shit. And they knew they didn't walk on the rain. You understand what I mean? Well, that's why all the people like, see all that sadness. Man, they didn't go for all that. And now, they made us play a whole lot of fat down a little number. My Blue Heaven. Catch many fellas right now.
You tell them to play them kind of numbers. I bet they can't play that. My Blue Heaven

and Trinidad Clover. Ask them can they play it. You catch many more and ask them can they play that. And that's a good number. That's a whole number. My Blue Heaven. You know where that number started? Right at the corner. At the very instance where they got a little ball in this corner, My Blue Heaven. Yeah. Yeah. Kid Howard, yeah. Kid Howard the one start the first playing that at the corner. When Howard was playing that, when Howard was playing that, when Howard was drunk, I'd go pick up Howard's horn and start the playing for him. See Howard was, you know, Howard would be playing that with Howard. He knew how he'd be drinking
like that. Yeah, you're scared. I go there and redeem, you understand what
I mean? And I see him and I start playing around there and helping him out like that. But I used to like all that. I like all that. You see, getting around them old fellas, you
can learn a whole lot from them. You can learn a whole lot from them old fellas. Those old fellas, did they play a lot of waltzes too? Yeah. Yeah, they play a lot of
things like that. You know, they don't know nothing about no waltzes. You catch all those
ladies, you catch them big bands, you never catch them playing no waltzes. Now they might,

now you catch them big bands that play like grand marches, grand marches like that, and marches like that. Well that's when they, the view of the people around them, whoever they're gonna get something in the hall, you understand what I mean? You march, play that, and after you play that, you play the Berlin Street Parade, and then they walk all around the hall like that.
There's nothing to it. There's nothing to it. What is it would make you good to see how to do that? Well in the old days I've heard how they played Gettysburg and some of those old marches.
Gettysburg. What did they do? The very first thing you'd play, would you start out with a march?
You start out with a march. See, you start with a march, and you swing around to a fox truck. Did everybody line up then with their party? You line up, no, you started dancing. You dance.
Even when you play the other way, they march around the hall, you understand? When you play in the fox town, well that's where I'd grab them and start dancing. That's right.
Man, that's a wonderful thing to see. What was the idea of them marching around the hall like that?

Well the idea, I tell you. You see, that's when they call it a call out. They be calling out the members for the guests. First what they do, all members is taking part in a dance. If you belong to the organization, they got a man with a book. He called Mrs. So-and-so, Mrs. Robert, or Mrs. Joan, or Mrs. Williams, and Mr. Williams. Well the ladies, there's 20 ladies, or 20 men, or 40 men, and 40 ladies. The ladies stand on one side. What you take and do them, when they call your name, they call the man's name first. When they call the man's name, they call the lady's name. Well you go and meet the lady and grab the lady by the arm. You understand? And you go marching, you stand right from the bandstand. Now they call somebody, well they have a souvenir there to give you. See they got a souvenir there to give you. Well I heard they do that at the carnival ball. Yeah they do that at all. Most of them dancers and dancers I'm talking about. They give you a souvenir. Give her a souvenir. Not the man, the lady. All right, you call yourself, give them your guests a guest. All right, they call their names when they give them a guest. She understands their dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear be dancing together. That's something nice to see. We're making all the parties be together, you understand what I mean, Bill? All together having fun. You'd be surprised to see something like that.
Does all these lodges do that?

Yeah, they still do that now. They still do that on and dance like that now. They call you out, it's a call I could call it. They call you out from you, your wife or your girlfriend, whoever you would. And sometimes they may have had a queen and a queen and little bridesmaids and little kids like that. They call them out first. They call them making it Dubuque. They make the Dubuque like that, you see. Well they open champagne, they pour it for them. Not for everybody. Everybody in that group was making the Dubuque, the girls. They have a college fellow serving, a tree, you know, serving all them champagne. That's just for the call out for the ones in the call out list. Well that might be about, say, about ten girls or ten men. That's something wonderful to see. Wonderful to see. You see them things, you'd be surprised to see something like that. That's all that get different. When you see them dancing, what I'm talking about, that's not anybody that can go to them dances. No, uh-uh. Unless you have an invitation. And they get so now, see them balls now, they make you be responsible for who you invite. One time I used to bring people with me and I'd go in there and play. You can't do that no more. Sometimes you bring them in there, you understand, the fellas make some bugger there. And they first thing they ask them, how did you get in there? They have a book with your name there in this book. The man who catch you, your name so-and-so and the kid, you got an invitation. Where do you get this invitation? Your name not on this book. Well you know that, that is embarrassing by the man. And so they have to do that. Now be careful not to let anybody come in on their parties. Well you don't know who can walk in on or dance on them. You understand what I mean? It's open houses, you don't see walking, you see nobody watching. Well they have this silver in there, they're right there giving it to you. You'd be surprised to see something like that.
So again, what about parades? You've played plenty of parades.
Oh yeah. I had a couple of pictures of them. Some of them I didn't know what come of them.
You still play them? Yeah, I still play them. With John Cadme.

Oh yeah. I played with John. I played with what you call this boy George Williams. You know. Well I tell you the truth, I'm going to be straight and tell you about them parades. That sun's been a little too hot man. I didn't know you were walking all that hot sun like that. It's hot in that sun man. It's always in the summertime. Yeah, it's hot in the summertime. It's hot. In the wintertime it was cool. I don't mind making it. Man, you know, do you know sometimes you be playing a parade, you know you can feel that heat coming through the caps, the white caps. Yeah, I know. You can feel that heat coming through that. And it, not, I ain't no use to be killing myself when I ain't got that to do.

You were talking about this street here used to be rocking. That's right, this would be rocking. Did you ever take parades on the streets like that? Sure they come through here. Sure they come through that. How did that affect you when you were marching playing? Just walking on the rocks is all you had to take and do.

Made it hard to blow. Yeah, it made it hard to blow. You're walking in holes, yeah, little holes like that. You understand me? They still got them, you know, they got them old stones in there. That's a long time. And you see, would you believe that? On that side of Claiborne Street, they got them big red bricks like that. They still got, they just got their eyes fell over. That's what this used to be, stone in the street out here. When I was a kid, it was nothing else with stones. And you walking down like that, your feet dipping in the mud, you know, going on a hole like that. You take a chance breaking your neck, you don't watch yourself.

That's the terrible thing. Well, did you ever play, you know, these funerals? I noticed these funerals, they play when they're reading the music. That'd be kind of tough to be walking and reading music too, wouldn't it?

No, it's not. No, it's not. Your breath, your breath, you have it up high. You don't be playing all that, you don't play. Them numbers most, they, they, you see what they're telling them? Them fellas don't be playing what's on that. They knows them numbers. They have it up there, but they don't be watching that. They knows it, they knows it. They know it. A man pick up a hymn, like Maryamagod the D, what friend we have in Jesus, they know you play it. All right, you know you know it. You know what key is written in. B flat, A flat, whatever it is, you know what key is in. You understand what I mean? Now what you call hard music to play, if you're playing a, like a sympathy orchestra. When a big military band like that with the music, it's hard. See, one time we played, John would tell you it was John Woodnette. I played for a bunch of white soldiers over the river. That was about a month ago. I believe we tried to get in touch with you all that. We left at Jackson Avenue. Well man, they come on some terrible marches, some 16, 168s. Boy, I'm hard to march with soldiers. If I know that y'all would like that, I'd never fool with it, you know. Man, do you know them soldiers like to walk over with us? They march fast, yeah. You know, I'm not lying, they like to walk clean overs. You can ask Alvin Alcon, Alvin was on the job too. Man, we're laying soldiers just four and five blocks, when we look, man, they're soldiers like that on top. Like that! And walk, walk, see when we stop, walking fast, and man, they're soldiers right up on us. Man, we told them, man, it's real, man, y'all, total captain, we couldn't total captain. You're all walking too fast for us. We didn't even train for about, man, I swear.
Man, you know them colored soldiers and white soldiers be right up on top of us? Yeah, I know, they can really step out of us. Man, they can walk, they can walk. They can walk.
They can walk, don't you know about the same thing, they can. Yeah, we always walk too fast.
Don't you know about them, them soldiers can't walk? They walk too fast.

Man, I was sure glad we got up the street up in the Kinner, or them up there, by the horse canal. Now, I'm glad. And then, I was so glad, and tell you all the time we spit, man, look like there's cotton coming out to us. It was so hot, we was thirsty, there's no way they could get no water, that's a stone white ball, and we couldn't stop, you understand? Well, we got out there, had a fair, some kind of fair, just giving to get some engines up there, you understand? I mean, they're giving them. What do you mean, they're playing money on this thing? And, man, we got up there, laid some soldiers, do you all mind drinking some beer? She didn't have to tell us that to once. She didn't have to tell us that to once, Bill. Boy, we was selling afterwards, we was selling that beer. We was selling that. Something to wet my throat now, so, see, when I had a couple of drinks that had been in me, I felt good after that. Man, I was so dry, and the soldiers, the soldiers already burned me up, walking all on top of me. Man, them people walking on the bill, I said, move the people right on top of you, walking on top of me. I said, no more playing nothing with no soldiers. I didn't know they marched like that. Yeah, they came really much down. The captain, now, look at that, and the captain, I said, wait, wait, I said, no, come on, Morgan, Morgan all in there, big, Morgan walking up, Morgan gripping like that. Morgan said, man, right back on us, right there. We left in there, we ain't on these blocks down there, Bill. Look at them, we ain't on these blocks, Bill. And, man, we look, see that man right up on us, and we was walking fast.
Yeah, yeah.

Walking fast, and then walking fast, and then it looked like, when you look down there, I said, man, we gonna walk in some water, it might cool our feet off. You think it's water, it looks like it's water down there by the mile. When you get there, that sun's so hot, man, that's the paper's so hot, it's a menu.
It's a button up. It shines, yeah.
Boy, that's something, man. So I said, well, I'm gonna let that alone. I don't want no more like that. I'm not them soldiers.
You know, they march you. Yeah, they march.
They march you.
They march too fast, yeah. They march too fast. I see an old man in there. I don't know how they made it. I know. It's a great job.
I know how they made it. I know. It's a great job. I know how they made it. I know. It's a great job. I know how they done it, Bill. I don't understand how they done it.
Well, they march.

They really go, yeah. They march. And they got there, they say, we play St. Louis Blues. We figure I make them slack up. Man, St. Louis Blues look like they're right on top of it. Man, dude, I just look at that and I say, no more dealing with the soldiers. She didn't have to ask me one time, do y'all care for something, Nick? Do we care for something, Nick? Man, they had a trough where they had water where they put horses full of it. She said, you always going to help yourself. She said, I know, Joe, you tired. I said, yes, ma'am, I am tired. I'm not tired. I'm tired and thirsty and everything. I wasn't starting to buy nothing. I want to get something to dry.
The inside was dry. Yeah, yeah, sure.

And you know, do you know this? You playing your horn, walking on the road like that. Do you know that, do you know your inside be dry as anything? Look like you make your trough be dry. Now that happened to us one time from the Cut-Off. You ever been going down to the Cut-Off? Oh, yeah. Down on the other side. Yeah. We played, I believe you was that son, we played at the parade.
I've been down there, yeah.
We played down there, walk from the Cut-Off to Algean, man.
Yeah, that's a lot. I said, no more job like that.
See, coming up, man, look like we don't get to town.
That's right, that's right.

And so, I told him, I said, man, no more. We see going back down there? I swear, Bill, we got down there so fast. I know how we got down there. Look like we used to fly down there. Going back, we made it fast. And do you know we didn't know, we got down there so fast? We coming up here? Sure. Didn't they? You know, guess what we were playing for? The horses and the cows in the field. The horses was dancing with one another. The cows. I didn't know what I was over there in the field. Yeah, you know that?
Yeah.
The horses dancing. The horses and cows running for one another. Yeah, really?
I've seen that.

That's right. And I said, now, Mick, now, I didn't give no credit on that. What they could have done is hire the truck to bring us up there and bring us back down there, we were playing a little longer down there. And we get down there, we had to play down there in a big open field for them.
All you're playing for the cows and the mules and horses and then dogs. You didn't see nothing in life.

Did you see anything? All you're seeing land, you understand, like pasture and all that. I said, man, if I knew it was going to be like that, I'd never come on no job like that. And I made a promise. I said, don't I'm playing music. If I know a job going to be something like that, you don't have no more trouble, you need to be going on them kind of jobs. And that's the hardest thing that's playing for you, you don't have nobody. Do you know you'd be more tired than you'd be working? See? And just like this jolly boy played this year. See, this year's what I mean they don't want to let them give no permit. They blocked up all the traffic.
Well, when is it going to, are they going to have one? No. Maybe they won't even have it, huh?

They ain't going to have it. They wouldn't give no permit. I wonder. Well, they overdo the thing. You understand what I mean? They block up all them buses. And that second line, they take us all over. You understand what I mean? They can have a parade like they're supposed to have it. No, they don't want to do right. They can have it and keep the traffic, keep out that traffic street with. Uh-huh.
Yeah.
Now, all jokes out. I play them white parades with Cornwall Parades. Them boys don't have no trouble. They don't have no traffic. No, that's right.
You got to give them.

They don't have no traffic. They parade goes on. They smooth and everything. And they come down a little busy street. One street be tied to be St. Charles. Well, they got it tied up on the counter for the wrecks. Yeah, yeah. Well, that's special. They got it special for that. Another thing. You see, we don't beat the wrecks at St. Charles and Louisiana Avenue. Yeah. You can't come down St. Charles. No, that's right. You got the wrecks that be most around Malcolm E. Coming up, we better be going down. See, the wreck is right. Even when we had Louisiana Avenue, you don't go down Louisiana Avenue. They don't let you go. You have to take the magazine. Go down the magazine. That's right. That's what I like about it. And you see, going down St. Charles, we be going. We just like horses going down there. Playing all the way, going all the time. The wrecks be coming up on one side and we coming down.
That's our life.

It's our life in the story of the bunch of musicians. And it's kicking, talking with one another and having fun. We talking about old things. And you see all those fellas you ain't seen in months a month, you think it's day to be living. On the corner down St. Charles Street. Some of them old time music. You see a lot of fellas.
